title: Advanced Developer Fundamentals
summary: Sharing, security, config, localization and patterns: the senior-dev toolbox for Apex that is safe, global and well designed.

lessons.title: Sharing Keywords: Who Sees Which Rows?
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, justify using sharing objects and Apex managed sharing (record-level access in Apex: with/without/inherited sharing)

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Some users may only see some records. **Sharing** is the set of rules for which records (rows) each user can see. By default Apex runs in **system mode**: it sees every record and skips the user's permissions. A **sharing keyword** on a class tells Apex whether to respect the user's record access.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A library card. `with sharing` checks your card, so you only get the books you may borrow. `without sharing` is the librarian's master key. Where it stops: the card only picks which books (rows). It never hides pages inside a book (fields).

cards.title: The three keywords
items: `with sharing`: respect the running user's sharing rules
`without sharing`: ignore sharing rules and see every row
`inherited sharing`: use the caller's mode; run `with sharing` when it is the entry point (the first class a request runs)

cards.title: Which one when?
items: `with sharing`: the safe default for code a user starts, like an LWC controller. A rep's list shows only the accounts they may see
`without sharing`: a small, targeted lift. A portal user must find records they can't see, like a matching case, so put just that query here
`inherited sharing`: service and utility classes that many callers share, so each caller decides

cards.title: No keyword?
cards.body: A class with **no keyword** takes the caller's mode when other Apex calls it. As an **entry point** it runs `without sharing`. One exception: `@AuraEnabled` controllers used by Lightning run `with sharing`. So always write a keyword. `inherited sharing` shows your intent clearly.

cards.title: Where the method lives wins
cards.body: The mode comes from the class where a method is **defined**, not the class that calls it. Say a `with sharing` class calls a method in a `without sharing` class. That method runs `without sharing`. An async job (like a Queueable) is a new entry point, so it doesn't inherit its caller's mode.

**Inner classes do NOT inherit** the outer class's keyword, so give each one its own. And `with sharing` **does NOT check CRUD or FLS** (object and field permissions). It only filters rows. Triggers can't take a keyword: they always run `without sharing`.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Sharing = Rows, Security = Columns.** Keywords pick the rows. `USER_MODE` and `stripInaccessible` guard the columns.

cards.title: Newer orgs (API 67.0+)
cards.body: The Apex Developer Guide says this changes at **API 67.0+**. Classes with no keyword run `with sharing`, and Apex runs in **user mode** by default. A class with no keyword that **extends** a parent takes the parent's mode. At 66.0 and earlier, the default is system mode. **Exam questions assume the classic behaviour unless they name the API version.**

terms.say: Sharing decides which records (rows) each user may see. Like a library card: it lets you borrow some books, but not all of them.
Apex's default way to run. It skips the user's object and field permissions. Whether it also skips record sharing depends on the class's sharing keyword.
A word on a class that tells Apex whether to respect the user's record access. There are three: with sharing, without sharing and inherited sharing.
The code only sees records the user may see. It filters rows only. It does not check object or field permissions.
The code ignores sharing rules and sees every record. Like the librarian's master key that opens every shelf.
Use the same mode as the code that called this class. If nothing called it, it runs with sharing. It shows your intent clearly.
The first Apex class a request runs, like the front door of a house. Nothing called it, so there is no caller mode to copy.
A tag that lets Lightning components call an Apex method. A class like that with no sharing keyword runs with sharing.
A class written inside another class. It does not copy the outer class's sharing keyword, so give it its own.
Telling the code: "act like the person using the app." Then it checks their object, field and record access, all three.

lessons.title: CRUD & FLS: Guard the Columns
lessons.objective: Enforce object- and field-level security in Apex (USER_MODE, WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED, Security.stripInaccessible, describe checks)

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Sharing decides which records you see. Two more locks decide the rest. **CRUD** asks: can you Create, Read, Update or Delete this object? **FLS** (field-level security) asks: which fields may you see or edit? Apex skips both by default. So your code must check them, or a user could see a field they shouldn't.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A spreadsheet with locked columns. Sharing hides some rows. FLS greys out some columns, like Salary. Your Apex is a helper with the master password, so it must choose to respect the locks. Where it stops: each tool below checks a different set of locks.

cards.title: User mode SOQL & DML
cards.body: These run the query and the saves in **user mode**, which checks object permissions, FLS **and** sharing. One keyword covers all three, and it fails loudly with an exception when access is missing. `WITH SYSTEM_MODE` and `as system` do the opposite. Salesforce recommends user mode for new code.

cards.title: `WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED` (older)
cards.body: This older SOQL clause checks **read** access only on fields in `SELECT` and `FROM`. It skips `WHERE` and `ORDER BY`, so a hidden field can still filter. It throws a `QueryException` at the first problem. It doesn't check sharing. Salesforce now recommends `WITH USER_MODE` instead.

cards.title: Strip instead of fail
cards.body: `stripInaccessible` quietly removes fields the user can't access and hands back clean copies. Use it when the work should still go on, like a form that saves only what the user may write. Save `getRecords()`, not the original list. Access types: `READABLE`, `CREATABLE`, `UPDATABLE`, `UPSERTABLE`. It doesn't support `AggregateResult`.

cards.title: Manual describe checks
cards.body: The classic check: ask the field's describe whether this user may edit it. It's handy for branching, like hiding an Edit button. Related: `isAccessible()` (read), `isCreateable()`, and `isDeletable()` on the object. Still valid, but wordy, and easy to forget a field.

cards.title: Which one when?
items: **New code that should fail if access is missing:** `WITH USER_MODE` and `as user`
**The work must go on, minus hidden fields:** `stripInaccessible`
**Show or hide one button or field:** describe checks like `isUpdateable()`
**Older code you maintain:** `WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED` (read checks only)

cards.body: Don't treat `USER_MODE` and `SECURITY_ENFORCED` as the same. `USER_MODE` also checks `WHERE` fields and enforces **sharing**. It can list **all** blocked fields with `QueryException.getInaccessibleFields()`.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Fail loud:** `USER_MODE` or `SECURITY_ENFORCED`. **Fail quiet:** `stripInaccessible`. Pick by whether the user should see an error.

terms.say: Sharing decides which records you can see. Like a class where you may open your own notebook, but not your friend's.
Four things you can do to records: Create (make one), Read (look at it), Update (change it), Delete (throw it away). CRUD says which of the four you may do.
Field-level security. Rules for single boxes on a record. You may see a person's name, but the Salary box can be hidden or locked for you.
Salesforce's own code. On its own, Apex acts like a grown-up with every key: it can see and change everything, even what the user can't. That's why you must tell it to check.
Telling the code: "act like the person using the app." Then it only sees and changes what that person may. It checks CRUD, FLS and sharing, all three.
How Apex asks the database a question, like "give me all Accounts named Acme." A clause is one part of that question, like WHERE (which ones) or ORDER BY (in what order).
The older way to make a query check. It only checks if you may read the fields you ask for. It forgets sharing and the WHERE part. If something isn't allowed, it stops with an error.
The error a query throws when it can't do what you asked. Like a door alarm: everything stops and it tells you what went wrong.
A quiet cleaner. You hand it records, it rubs out the fields the user may not touch, and gives you clean copies. No error, no alarm. Save the clean copies, not the originals.
Asking Salesforce about something, like "what is this field, and may this user edit it?" Like reading the label on a box before you open it.

lessons.title: Apex Managed Sharing
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, justify using sharing objects and Apex managed sharing

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Sometimes the point-and-click tools can't say who should see a record. **OWD** (org-wide default, everyone's starting access), roles, sharing rules and teams all fall short. Then code writes the access itself. That is **Apex managed sharing**. Example: share a project with every user listed in its child records.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A guest list for a party. Each **share record** is one line: this guest, this party, this level of access. Code adds and removes lines. Where it stops: the list can't hand out the host's own keys. The top level, **All**, belongs to the owner only.

cards.title: A share row
cards.body: Insert one share row to give one user or group access. Each field answers a question: `ParentId` is which record, `UserOrGroupId` is who, `AccessLevel` is how much (**Read** or **Edit**), and `RowCause` is why. A custom object's share object is `ObjectName__Share`.

cards.title: Share object facts
items: A custom object has one only if its OWD is **Private** or **Public Read Only**
A share must grant **more** than the OWD, so Read on Public Read Only fails
Master-detail children have none (**Controlled by Parent**): share the master
`AccessLevel` **All** is for the owner only
Standard objects use their own fields, like `AccountId` and `AccountAccessLevel`

cards.title: `RowCause` matters
cards.body: `RowCause` says why a share exists. The default is **Manual**, and Manual shares are **deleted when the owner changes**. A custom **Apex sharing reason** (set up on custom objects) keeps shares through owner changes. Strictly, only reason shares count as Apex managed sharing. Only users with **Modify All Data** can edit or delete those shares in the UI.

cards.title: Recalculation
cards.body: Shares can go missing, for example when record locking blocks a write. So you register a `Database.Batchable` class under the object's **Apex Sharing Recalculation**. It runs when the object's OWD changes or when an admin starts it. `Database.executeBatch` can start it too. It should only rebuild shares with its own `RowCause`.

Don't mix up a share record with a `without sharing` class. `without sharing` only lets **your code** see more rows, during that one request. A share gives the **user** real access everywhere: the record page, list views and reports. The user must open the record? Write a share. Only the code must read it? Use `without sharing`.

You can't move a share by editing it. `ParentId`, `UserOrGroupId` and `RowCause` **are fixed** after insert. Only `AccessLevel` can change. To give access to someone else, delete the old share and insert a new one.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Manual melts, Reasons remain.** An owner change melts Manual shares. Apex sharing reasons survive.

terms.say: Org-wide default. Everyone's starting access to one object's records, like Private or Public Read Only. Sharing can only open more, never less.
Code that gives people access to records when the click tools can't. It writes share records itself, like adding names to a guest list.
One line on the guest list: this user or group may see this record, with this level of access.
The list that holds a custom object's share records. Its name ends in __Share, like Project__Share.
How much a share gives: Read (look) or Edit (change). All (full control) belongs to the record's owner only.
The reason a share exists, written on the share itself. It decides whether the share survives when the record gets a new owner.
The default reason on a share. Manual shares are deleted when the record's owner changes, like a new host tearing up the old guest list.
A custom reason you create for your code's shares, on custom objects only. These shares stay when the owner changes. Only users with Modify All Data (a top admin power) can edit them in the UI.
The child in a master-detail link just follows its parent's access. So it has no share object of its own. Share the parent (master) instead.
Where you register a batch class (code that works through many records in chunks) to rebuild your code's shares. It runs when the OWD changes or an admin starts it.

lessons.title: Custom Metadata vs Settings vs Labels
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, choose between custom metadata types, custom settings, and custom labels for configuration

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Good code keeps changeable values out of the code. Tax rates, limits and messages live in config instead. Salesforce gives you three homes for them: **custom metadata types**, **custom settings** and **custom labels**. The exam asks which one fits each job.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A restaurant chain. **Custom metadata** is the printed menu: it ships to every branch. **Custom settings** are one branch's specials board: written there, never shipped. **Custom labels** are the menu translated for each guest. Where it stops: hierarchy settings can also change per profile or per user.

cards.title: Custom metadata types (`__mdt`)
cards.body: Their records **are metadata**, so they deploy with change sets, packages or the CLI. Apex, formulas, validation rules and flows can read them. **Tests see them** without `SeeAllData`. Mark the type **Protected** in a managed package, and only code in that namespace can read the records.

cards.title: Read CMT without SOQL
cards.code:
Discount__mdt gold = Discount__mdt.getInstance('Gold');
Map<String, Discount__mdt> all = Discount__mdt.getAll();
cards.body: These read records with no SOQL, but return only the **first 255 characters** of each field. Plain SOQL on custom metadata doesn't count toward the SOQL limit either, except long text area fields.

cards.title: Changing CMT from Apex
cards.body: You can't insert or update `__mdt` records with DML. Build a `Metadata.CustomMetadata` object and call `Metadata.Operations.enqueueDeployment()`. It is **asynchronous** (it finishes later) and reports back through a `Metadata.DeployCallback`. Use it for admin setup screens or install scripts, not for values that change all the time: each change is a small deployment.

cards.title: Custom settings (`__c`)
items: **Hierarchy**: org, then profile, then user. `getInstance()` returns the most specific value for each field
**List**: one org-wide lookup table. Use `getAll()` or `getInstance(name)`
Cached, and normal DML works
Data is **not** deployed and **not visible in tests**: insert it in the test
Formulas can read only hierarchy settings, through `$Setup`
Not for secrets: unprotected settings can be read by every profile, even guests

cards.title: Custom labels
cards.body: Labels are text you can **translate** in the **Translation Workbench**. Apex reads `System.Label.My_Label`. LWC imports `@salesforce/label/c.My_Label`. Example: an "Out of stock" error appears as "Rupture de stock" to a French user. Use labels for messages people read, not for logic settings.

Settings and metadata both feel like config, but act in opposite ways. **Custom setting data** doesn't deploy, and tests can't see it. **Custom metadata records** deploy, and tests can see them, but you can't insert your own with DML.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Metadata moves, Settings stay, Labels speak.** Metadata deploys. Setting data stays in its org. Labels talk to users in their own language. Value per profile or user? Hierarchy setting.

terms.say: Settings saved as metadata, like a printed menu sent to every branch. They deploy with your code, and tests can see them. Code can't insert them with DML.
Settings saved as data in one org, like one shop's specials board. The data doesn't deploy, and tests can't see it unless the test inserts it.
Short texts, like messages, that can be translated into each user's language. Use them for words people read, not for logic settings.
A custom setting with three layers: org, then profile, then user. The most specific value wins, like a person's own rule beating the company rule.
A lock on custom metadata in a managed package (an app installed from someone else). Only that package's own code can read the records.
A test setting that lets a test see the org's real data. Custom metadata doesn't need it: tests see those records anyway.
The Apex statements that save changes to records: insert, update and delete. Like writing in the database with a pen.
How Apex changes custom metadata records. It sends them off to deploy, and the work finishes later. A callback (code that runs when it's done) tells you how it went.
Reads a custom setting. For a hierarchy setting, it gives the most specific value for each field: the user's, else the profile's, else the org's.
How a formula reads a hierarchy custom setting. Formulas can't read list custom settings at all.

lessons.title: Locales, Currencies & Time Zones
lessons.objective: Demonstrate knowledge of localization and multi-currency features and capabilities and how they affect coding

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Your users live in different places. They write dates, numbers and money differently, and their clocks differ. **Locale** (a user's country and format style), **time zone** and **currency** settings handle this. Your code must respect them, or a Tokyo user sees the wrong month.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: An airport departures board. Every flight time is kept on one master clock, **GMT**. Each screen shows it in local time and local style. Where it stops: SOQL date functions read the master clock (UTC) unless you ask for local time.

cards.title: `Datetime` = GMT inside
cards.body: **Datetimes are stored in GMT.** `format()` shows them in the user's **time zone** and **locale**. `formatGmt()` keeps GMT. `date()` gives the user's local date, and `dateGmt()` the GMT date. Example: 23:30 GMT on 1 May is already 2 May in Tokyo. A `Date` has no time zone. `Date.parse()` follows the user's locale. `Date.valueOf()` reads `yyyy-MM-dd`.

cards.title: Know your user
cards.body: Read the user's time zone, locale and currency at run time instead of hard-coding them. The same code then serves a user in Tokyo and one in Berlin. `getLocale()` returns a code like `en_US`, and `getDefaultCurrency()` a code like `EUR`.

cards.title: Localize in SOQL
cards.code:
SELECT toLabel(StageName),
       FORMAT(convertCurrency(Amount)) amt
FROM Opportunity
cards.body: `toLabel` gives the picklist value in the user's language. `convertCurrency` turns the amount into the user's currency, and `FORMAT` writes it in their local style (decimal marks, currency). Give a wrapped field an alias, like `amt`.

cards.title: Multi-currency in code
cards.body: With **multi-currency** on, each record gets a `CurrencyIsoCode` field naming its currency. Rates live in `CurrencyType`. Dated rates live in `DatedConversionRate` (advanced currency management only). A new record takes its creator's currency. Aggregates with `GROUP BY` return the **corporate currency**. Multi-currency **can't be turned off**.

Writing `CurrencyIsoCode` directly in code won't compile in orgs without multi-currency. Why: the field exists only when multi-currency is on, and Apex checks field names when it compiles. In packages, check `UserInfo.isMultiCurrencyOrganization()` first. Then use dynamic SOQL or `sObject.get('CurrencyIsoCode')`.

SOQL date functions like `CALENDAR_MONTH` and `DAY_ONLY` use **UTC**. Wrap the field in `convertTimezone()` to group by local time. And `convertCurrency()` is **not allowed** in `WHERE` or `ORDER BY`. Filter with a literal like `USD100000` instead.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Store in GMT, show in local.** Format for people, never for storage or parsing.

terms.say: A user's country and format style. It decides how dates, numbers and money look, like 12/31 in one place and 31/12 in another.
Where the user's clock is set, like Tokyo or London. The same moment shows a different hour in each.
One master clock for the whole world. Salesforce stores every date-and-time on it. UTC is practically the same clock.
A date plus a time, like a flight's departure. It is stored in GMT, and format() shows it in the user's local time.
A SOQL word that gives a picklist value (a choice from a dropdown) translated into the user's language.
A SOQL word that shows an amount in the user's own currency. It's not allowed in WHERE or ORDER BY, so filter with a literal like USD100000.
An org setting that lets records use different money, like dollars and euros. Once it's turned on, it can never be turned off.
The field naming a record's currency, like USD or EUR. It exists only with multi-currency on, so code naming it directly won't compile in other orgs.
The company's main currency. Totals from GROUP BY queries come back in it, not in each record's own currency.
Turns a stored GMT time into the user's local time inside a SOQL date function. Use it to group records by local day or hour.

lessons.title: Dynamic Apex & Schema Describe
lessons.objective: Use dynamic Apex, Schema describe information, and Apex type behaviour to build flexible, safe code

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Sometimes code doesn't know until run time which object, field or class it needs. **Dynamic Apex** handles that. **Schema describe** asks Salesforce about objects and fields, like reading the label on a box. It gives facts without queries, so you can build flexible tools without hard-coding names.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A vending machine that takes a typed code. You type B4, and it finds the snack at run time. Where it stops: if typed text goes into a SOQL string, a bad user can type extra query words. That's **SOQL injection**, so bind the input.

cards.title: Describe without SOQL
cards.body: Get record type IDs and field maps from describes, not from queries or hard-coded IDs. Why: record type IDs differ between sandbox and production, so a hard-coded ID breaks after a deploy. `recordId.getSObjectType()` also names a record's object cheaply.

cards.title: Safe dynamic SOQL
cards.body: **Bind variables** pass user input as data, so it can't change the query. With `queryWithBinds`, the values travel in a map and the query text never changes. `String.escapeSingleQuotes()` is the fallback when you must glue strings together.

cards.title: Pick a class at runtime
cards.code:
Type t = Type.forName(cfg.Handler_Class__c);
DiscountStrategy s = (DiscountStrategy) t.newInstance();
cards.body: `Type.forName` finds a class by name and returns `null` if it doesn't exist. `newInstance()` needs a public no-argument constructor. Why: store the class name in custom metadata, and admins swap the logic without a code change. Cast to an interface, and check for `null` first.

cards.title: Generic sObject access
cards.body: `rec.get('Field__c')` and `rec.put('Field__c', v)` read and write a field by name. `rec.getSObject('Account')` follows a relationship. `newSObject()` on a type token makes a new record. **Don't call** `Schema.getGlobalDescribe()` **in loops**, because it is expensive.

cards.title: Type gotchas
items: `'abc' == 'ABC'` is `true` (`==` ignores case)
`'abc'.equals('ABC')` is `false`
`Set` and `Map` `String` keys are **case-sensitive**
`7 / 2` on Integers is **3**
`List<Account>` `instanceof` `List<SObject>` is true
A list made as `new List<SObject>()` can't be cast to `List<Account>`

cards.body: Stripping spaces or adding a `LIMIT` does nothing against injection. `String.escapeSingleQuotes()` is only a fallback. **Bind variables** are the robust fix. But binds only carry values: if input picks a field or object name, check it against the describe field map (an allow-list).

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Describe, don't query. Bind, don't glue.**

terms.say: Code that picks the object, field or class while it runs, not when you write it. Like a vending machine that finds the snack from the code you type.
Asking Salesforce about objects and fields: names, types, record types. Like reading the label on a box. It needs no SOQL query.
A trick where a bad user types query words into a text box. If code glues that text into a query, the query does something you never meant.
A slot in a query, written :name, that takes user input as plain data. The input can never change the query itself. It's the safest fix for injection.
Puts a backslash before each single quote in user text, so the text can't end the query string early. A fallback; bind variables are better.
Finds a class by its name while the code runs. If no class has that name, it returns null (nothing).
Makes a new object from a type found at run time. The class needs a public constructor (its setup code) that takes no inputs.
A value that stands for an object type, like Account. Call newSObject() on it to make a new, empty record of that type.
Gives a map of every object in the org. It is slow and expensive, so call it once, never inside a loop.
Asks: is this value of that type? Like asking: is this pet a dog? A list of Accounts counts as a list of any records (List<SObject>).

lessons.title: OOP & Design Patterns
lessons.objective: Apply object-oriented Apex (interfaces, abstract and virtual classes) and common design patterns

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: **OOP** (object-oriented programming) means building code from classes that share and reuse behaviour. **Design patterns** are proven recipes for arranging those classes. They keep a big org tidy, testable and easy to change.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: LEGO. An **interface** is the stud shape: anything that fits can plug in. An `abstract` class is a half-built kit: a child must add the last pieces. A `virtual` class is a finished model you may remodel. Where it stops: in Apex, a plain class comes glued shut (`final`).

cards.title: Class flavours
items: Classes are `final` **by default**: no one can extend them
`virtual`: can be extended AND created with `new`
`abstract`: can be extended, never created; may mix `abstract` and finished methods
**interface**: method signatures only; a class can implement many. The class's methods that fulfil it must be `public` or `global`

cards.title: Overriding
cards.body: To replace a method, the parent method must be `virtual` or `abstract`, and the child must say `override`. Calls made inside the parent still run the child's version.

cards.title: Trigger handler
cards.body: Use **one trigger per object**, with no logic inside it. The trigger hands work to a handler class that routes by context, like `before insert` or `after update`. You get a predictable order, easy tests, and one place for recursion guards.

cards.title: Enterprise layers (fflib)
items: **Service**: business operations; owns the transaction
**Domain**: object-specific logic and validation
**Selector**: all SOQL for an object in one place
**Unit of Work**: collects DML and commits it in one go
cards.body: Why: each layer has one job, so you can test or swap one without touching the others.

cards.title: Singleton & Strategy
cards.body: **Singleton**: one shared instance, made by a `private` constructor and a `static` `getInstance()`. It lasts only **one transaction**, because statics reset per request, even in a `Database.Stateful` batch. **Strategy**: an interface with swappable classes, often picked at run time with `Type.forName`.
Several triggers on one object run in **no guaranteed order**, and Apex has no trigger-order setting. The fix is one trigger per object plus a handler. A static flag only stops recursion.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Virtual = Very flexible, Abstract = Almost done.** An `abstract` class needs a child to finish it. Only a contract for unrelated classes? Interface. Shared code too? Abstract or virtual.

terms.say: A list of methods a class promises to have, with no code inside. Like a plug shape: anything that fits can plug in. A class can use many.
A half-built class. You can't create one with new. A child class must extend it and finish its abstract methods.
A class or method that children may extend or change. A virtual class can also be created with new, unlike an abstract one.
Closed: no one can extend it. Apex classes and methods are final unless you mark them virtual or abstract.
The word a child class writes to replace its parent's method. The parent method must be virtual or abstract.
The class a trigger hands all its work to. The trigger stays empty, and the handler picks what to do for each event, like before insert.
One class that holds all the SOQL queries for one object. Like one librarian who fetches every book of one kind.
Collects all the record changes during a job, then saves them in one go at the end. Like a shopping cart you pay for once.
A class with only one shared copy. Its constructor is private, so code gets the copy from a static getInstance(). The copy lasts only one transaction (one request).
Several swappable classes behind one interface, each doing the job its own way. Code picks one, often at run time with Type.forName.

lessons.title: Exceptions & Savepoints
lessons.objective: Implement exception handling, custom exceptions, and transaction control with savepoints

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Things go wrong: a save fails, or a record is bad. **Exceptions** are how Apex reports the problem. **Savepoints** let you undo part of your work, like an undo button for database changes. Together they keep data clean when something breaks.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A video game checkpoint. `setSavepoint()` saves a checkpoint. `rollback()` sends you back and undoes every database change since. Where it stops: your static variables and record IDs aren't reset. Only the database is rewound.

cards.title: Custom exception
cards.code:
public class OrderException extends Exception {}

throw new OrderException('Out of stock');
cards.body: Extend `Exception`, and the class name **must end in "Exception"**. You get message and cause constructors for free. Why bother: callers can catch your exact problem with `catch (OrderException e)` and let other errors pass.

cards.title: Savepoint & rollback
cards.body: If a save fails, undo all DML since the savepoint, then throw your own exception that keeps the original as its cause. Rethrowing tells the caller it failed. Swallowing the error would hide it.

cards.title: Savepoint gotchas
items: `setSavepoint` and `rollback` **each count** toward the DML statement limit
IDs on rolled-back records are **not cleared**, so inserting them again fails
**Static variables are not reverted**
Rolling back to an earlier savepoint makes later ones **invalid**

cards.title: Partial success
cards.body: `Database.insert(recs, false)` saves the good records and returns `SaveResult[]` instead of throwing. Use it for imports and integrations, where one bad row shouldn't block 199 good ones. Loop over them and check `isSuccess()` and `getErrors()`. In triggers, use `addError()` to block one record with a friendly message.

cards.title: Logs that survive
cards.body: An **uncaught exception** rolls back the whole transaction, including any error log you just inserted. To keep a log anyway, publish a **platform event set to Publish Immediately**. It goes out even when the transaction rolls back.
`System.LimitException` **can't be caught.** A `try/catch` won't rescue a limit error. Check `Limits.getQueries()` and similar methods before you reach the limit, and bulkify your code.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Rewind the data, not the variables.** Rollback rewinds only the database. And limits can't be caught, only avoided.

terms.say: Apex's way of shouting "something went wrong!" It stops the normal flow until code catches it. Your own exception classes must end in the word Exception.
A checkpoint in your database work, like in a video game. Later you can go back to it and undo what came after.
Goes back to a savepoint and undoes every database change made since. Variables and record IDs stay as they were. It counts toward the DML (save) statement limit.
Saves the good records and skips the bad ones, instead of failing them all. It hands back a result for each record to check.
The report card for one record after a Database save. isSuccess() says if it saved. getErrors() says what went wrong.
Used in a trigger to block one record from saving. It shows the user a friendly error message on that record.
An error that no code catches. It ends the request and undoes all its database changes, even the error log you just saved.
A message Salesforce sends out to listeners. Set to Publish Immediately, it goes out at once, even if the rest of the work is undone.
The error when code goes over a governor limit (a usage cap). It can't be caught. The only cure is staying under the limit.
Writing code that handles many records at once. Query and save whole lists in one go, never one record at a time inside a loop.

lessons.title: Platform Cache Basics
lessons.objective: Describe Platform Cache (org and session cache) and when it improves governor-limit-aware design

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Some data is slow to fetch but read all the time, like exchange rates. **Platform Cache** keeps a copy in fast memory, so you skip repeat queries. It is a short-term store, not a database. It helps you stay under **governor limits** (the platform's usage caps per transaction).

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A sticky note on the fridge with the pizza place's number. It's faster than looking it up each time. Where it stops: someone may throw the note away at any moment. So always be ready to look the number up again.

cards.title: Two caches
items: **Org cache**: shared by all users; default TTL (time to live) 24 hours, max 48 hours
**Session cache**: tied to one user's session; max 8 hours
Space is split into **partitions**
Statics last one transaction; cache lasts across requests

cards.title: Put & get
cards.body: Get a partition, store a value for an hour, read it back, and reload on a miss. Keys must be alphanumeric. `local` means your org's own namespace.

cards.title: `CacheBuilder` = auto-load on miss
cards.body: One call does get-or-load: on a miss, `doLoad()` runs and its result is cached for you. Your class implements `Cache.CacheBuilder`, and the key is passed to `doLoad()`. The caller never writes the miss check.
Cache is **not guaranteed**. Entries can be evicted (thrown out) before the TTL ends, and changing an Apex class can clear the cache. **Always handle null (a cache miss)** and reload from the source.

cards.title: Two more rules
cards.body: With **no default partition**, a key without a partition name throws `Cache.Org.OrgCacheException`. Use `local.Rates.usdEur` or `getPartition()`. Cached data **isn't encrypted**, so never cache secrets like payment tokens.

cards.title: Good to know
items: If the transaction fails, its cache writes roll back too
A full partition is **evicted** oldest-used first: the least recently used keys go
One cached item can be at most **100 KB**. Cache a few bigger items, not many tiny ones
Call `get()` and check for `null`. Calling `contains()` first wastes a trip

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: Cache what is **read often, changes rarely, and costs a lot to build**: config, rates, describe results. Don't cache data that must be exact right now.

terms.say: Fast short-term memory in Salesforce. You keep a copy of slow-to-get data there, so you don't fetch it again. Like a sticky note on the fridge.
Caps on how much one transaction (one request) may use, like how many queries it runs. Go over one, and everything stops.
Cache shared by all users in the org. Values live 24 hours by default, and 48 hours at most.
Cache tied to one user's login session. Only that session sees it, and it lasts 8 hours at most.
Time to live: how long a cached value may stay before it expires. Like a best-before date. It can still be thrown out earlier.
A named slice of your cache space, like one shelf in the fridge. Without a default partition, every key must name its partition.
Asking the cache for something that isn't there, so you get null (nothing). Then fetch it from the source and store it again.
The method you write in a CacheBuilder class. On a cache miss it runs and loads the value, and the cache keeps the result for you.
Thrown out of the cache early, before its time is up. It can happen any time, so never count on a value staying.
A name meaning your own org's namespace (its name tag). Write it before the partition name, like local.Rates.

flashcards.front: What does `with sharing` do?
flashcards.back: It makes the class respect the running user's record access, so queries only see rows the user may see. It does NOT check CRUD or FLS.

flashcards.front: How does a class with no sharing keyword run?
flashcards.back: Called by other Apex, it takes the caller's mode. As an entry point it runs `without sharing`, except `@AuraEnabled` (Lightning) controllers, which run `with sharing`. Classic rule; API 67.0+ defaults to `with sharing`.

flashcards.front: What does `inherited sharing` do?
flashcards.back: It uses the caller's sharing mode. When it is the entry point, it runs `with sharing`. It is the recommended default for shared utility classes.

flashcards.front: Does an inner class inherit its outer class's sharing keyword?
flashcards.back: No. An inner class doesn't copy its outer class's keyword, so give each inner class its own. Otherwise it follows the rules for a class with no keyword.

flashcards.front: What does `WITH USER_MODE` check in a query?
flashcards.back: Everything the user is allowed: CRUD, FLS (`WHERE` fields too) and sharing. It can list all blocked fields with `getInaccessibleFields()`.

flashcards.front: What does `WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED` check, and what does it miss?
flashcards.back: It checks read access on `SELECT` and `FROM` fields only, then throws a `QueryException`. It misses `WHERE` fields and sharing. Salesforce prefers `USER_MODE` now.

flashcards.front: What does `Security.stripInaccessible()` do?
flashcards.back: It quietly removes fields the user can't access instead of throwing. It returns an `SObjectAccessDecision`: `getRecords()` gives the clean copies, `getRemovedFields()` lists what was dropped.

flashcards.front: How do you write DML in user mode?
flashcards.back: Write `insert as user rec;` or `Database.insert(rec, AccessLevel.USER_MODE);`. Both check CRUD and FLS.

flashcards.front: What is a custom object's share object called, and what are its fields?
flashcards.back: `ObjectName__Share`. Fields: `ParentId` (the record), `UserOrGroupId` (who), `AccessLevel` (Read or Edit) and `RowCause` (why).

flashcards.front: When does a custom object have a share object?
flashcards.back: Only when its OWD is Private or Public Read Only. There is none for Public Read/Write or Controlled by Parent.

flashcards.front: What happens to shares when a record's owner changes?
flashcards.back: Manual shares are deleted. Shares with a custom Apex sharing reason (custom objects only) survive.

flashcards.front: What is an Apex sharing recalculation class?
flashcards.back: A `Database.Batchable` class registered on the custom object. It runs when the OWD changes or when an admin starts it, and rebuilds the shares.

flashcards.front: What is a custom metadata type, in one line?
flashcards.back: Config records that deploy like metadata (`__mdt`). Apex reads them with `getAll()` or `getInstance()` and no SOQL, and tests can see them.

flashcards.front: How does Apex create or update custom metadata records?
flashcards.back: Through the Metadata API: `Metadata.Operations.enqueueDeployment()`. It runs asynchronously. DML isn't allowed on `__mdt`.

flashcards.front: How does a hierarchy custom setting pick its value?
flashcards.back: It layers org, then profile, then user values. `getInstance()` returns the most specific value for the running user.

flashcards.front: Can a test see custom setting data?
flashcards.back: Not by default. Custom setting records count as data, and tests can't see org data. Insert the records in the test or in test setup.

flashcards.front: How do you read a custom label in Apex and in LWC?
flashcards.back: Apex: `System.Label.Name`. LWC: `import x from '@salesforce/label/c.Name'`. Labels are translatable.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between `Datetime.format()` and `formatGmt()`?
flashcards.back: `format()` shows the time in the user's time zone and locale. `formatGmt()` keeps it in GMT.

flashcards.front: What does `convertCurrency()` do in SOQL?
flashcards.back: It returns currency fields converted to the user's currency. It works only in multi-currency orgs, and it isn't allowed in `WHERE` or `ORDER BY`.

flashcards.front: What do `toLabel()` and `FORMAT()` do in SOQL?
flashcards.back: `toLabel()` returns the translated picklist label. `FORMAT()` returns a number, date or currency in the user's locale format.

flashcards.front: Why wrap a field in `convertTimezone()`?
flashcards.back: SOQL date functions group by UTC. Wrapping the datetime in `convertTimezone()` makes them group by the user's local time.

flashcards.front: How should a package use `CurrencyIsoCode` safely?
flashcards.back: A direct reference won't compile without multi-currency. Check `isMultiCurrencyOrganization()`, then use dynamic SOQL or `get('CurrencyIsoCode')`.

flashcards.front: How do you stop SOQL injection?
flashcards.back: Pass user input as a bind variable, for example with `Database.queryWithBinds()`. The fallback is `String.escapeSingleQuotes()`.

flashcards.front: What does `Type.forName()` do?
flashcards.back: It finds an Apex class by name at run time, and `newInstance()` creates one. It returns `null` if no class has that name.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between `virtual` and `abstract` classes?
flashcards.back: `virtual`: you can extend it AND create it with `new`. `abstract`: you can only extend it. A plain class is `final` by default.

flashcards.front: What are the rules for a custom exception?
flashcards.back: It must extend `Exception`, and its name must end in "Exception". Why use one: callers can catch your exact error type.

flashcards.front: Can you catch a `LimitException`?
flashcards.back: No. `System.LimitException` skips every catch block and ends the transaction. Avoid it: bulkify, and check the `Limits` class (like `Limits.getQueries()`) before you get close.

flashcards.front: What does a savepoint rollback NOT undo?
flashcards.back: It doesn't clear record IDs or reset static variables. Also, `setSavepoint()` and `rollback()` each count toward the DML limit.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between org cache and session cache?
flashcards.back: Org cache is shared by all users, max TTL 48 hours. Session cache belongs to one user session, max 8 hours. Always handle a miss.

flashcards.front: How do you find a record's object type from its Id cheaply?
flashcards.back: Call `recordId.getSObjectType()`. It returns the token, like `Account.SObjectType`, with no SOQL and no global describe.

flashcards.front: What happens with a cache key that has no partition, and no default partition exists?
flashcards.back: It throws `Cache.Org.OrgCacheException`. Use a full key like `local.Partition.key`, or call `getPartition()` first.

questions.q: A `with sharing` class `OrderController` calls `OrderUtil.getOpenOrders()`. `OrderUtil` has no sharing keyword. Under which sharing mode does the query in `getOpenOrders()` run?
options: `without sharing`, because a class with no keyword always runs in system mode
`with sharing`, because `OrderUtil` inherits the calling class's mode
It depends on the user's profile permissions
Compile error: the called class must declare a sharing keyword
questions.explain: A class with no sharing keyword copies the mode of the Apex that calls it. `OrderController` is `with sharing`, so the query in `getOpenOrders()` respects sharing too. (At API 67.0+ a class with no keyword runs `with sharing` anyway, so the answer is the same.)
wrong: No keyword doesn't mean `without sharing`. When other Apex calls it, it copies the caller's mode.
Profiles don't pick the sharing mode. The class keywords do.
The keyword is optional, so the class compiles fine without one.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Using the with sharing, without sharing, and inherited sharing Keywords

questions.q: A utility class is used two ways: called from `without sharing` batch classes, and as the entry point of a REST endpoint (`@RestResource`) used by a partner app. As the REST entry point it must respect the user's record access. When called by other Apex it must adopt the caller's mode. Which declaration meets both needs?
options: `public without sharing class RecordUtil`
`public class RecordUtil` (no keyword)
`public with sharing class RecordUtil`
`public inherited sharing class RecordUtil`
questions.explain: You need a class that copies its caller, but respects sharing when it starts the request itself. That is exactly `inherited sharing`: the caller's mode from other Apex, and `with sharing` as an entry point like a REST request.
wrong: This ignores sharing for the REST user too.
No keyword copies the caller, but as a REST entry point it runs `without sharing`.
This always enforces sharing, even when a `without sharing` batch calls it.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Using the inherited sharing Keyword

questions.q: Which two statements about Apex sharing keywords are true? (Choose 2)
options: An inner class does not inherit the `with sharing` setting of its outer class
A `with sharing` class automatically enforces field-level security on its SOQL queries
The sharing mode of the class where a method is defined applies when that method runs
Triggers run `with sharing` by default
A `without sharing` class cannot be called from a `with sharing` class
questions.explain: Each class sets its own sharing mode. Inner classes need their own keyword, and a method runs in the mode of the class that defines it, whoever calls it.
wrong: Sharing keywords only filter records. FLS needs `USER_MODE`, `stripInaccessible` or describe checks.
Triggers run `without sharing`, in system context.
Mixing modes is allowed. The defining class's mode applies to its method.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Using the with sharing, without sharing, and inherited sharing Keywords

questions.q: A developer is writing a SOQL query for a public-facing component. It must enforce the running user's object permissions, field-level security (including fields in the `WHERE` clause), and record sharing, all in one statement. What should the developer use?
options: `WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED`
A `with sharing` class and no query clause
`Security.stripInaccessible(AccessType.READABLE, ...)`
`WITH USER_MODE`
questions.explain: Only one clause checks object permissions, every field and sharing at once. `WITH USER_MODE` checks CRUD, FLS (`WHERE` fields included) and sharing for that query.
wrong: `SECURITY_ENFORCED` checks only `SELECT` and `FROM` fields, and it skips sharing.
Sharing keywords don't check CRUD or FLS.
`stripInaccessible` cleans results after the query. It doesn't check `WHERE` fields or sharing.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Enforce User Mode for Database Operations

questions.q: The running user has Read access on Account but no field-level access to `Credit_Score__c`. What happens when this code runs?
options: The query returns accounts with `Credit_Score__c` set to `null`
A `System.QueryException` is thrown
The query returns accounts and `Credit_Score__c` is silently removed from the `SELECT`
A `System.NoAccessException` is thrown only when the code reads `Credit_Score__c`
questions.explain: `WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED` fails loudly. `Credit_Score__c` is in the `SELECT` and the user can't read it, so the query throws a `QueryException`. It never strips fields.
wrong: It doesn't blank out the field. The whole query fails.
Quiet stripping is what `Security.stripInaccessible` does, not this clause.
The query itself fails before any field is read.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Filter SOQL Queries Using WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED

questions.q: A developer must insert records built from an external JSON payload. The running user's object permissions and field-level security must be enforced on the insert. Which two approaches meet this? (Choose 2)
options: `insert as user records;`
Declare the class `with sharing` and use `insert records;`
Add `WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED` to the insert statement
`Database.insert(records, false);`
`Database.insert(records, AccessLevel.USER_MODE);`
questions.explain: To check permissions on a save, run the DML in **user mode**. Both `insert as user` and `Database.insert` with `AccessLevel.USER_MODE` check CRUD and FLS.
wrong: `with sharing` only filters records. It doesn't check CRUD or FLS.
`WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED` belongs in SOQL, not in DML.
`allOrNone = false` allows partial success. It doesn't check permissions.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Enforce User Mode for Database Operations

questions.q: Before setting `Contact.Email` in Apex, a developer wants to manually confirm that the running user is allowed to edit that field. Which check is correct?
options: `Schema.sObjectType.Contact.fields.Email.isAccessible()`
`Schema.sObjectType.Contact.fields.Email.isPermissionable()`
`Schema.sObjectType.Contact.fields.Email.isUpdateable()`
`UserInfo.canEdit(Contact.Email)`
questions.explain: To edit a field, ask whether the user may update it. `isUpdateable()` on the field describe checks edit access (FLS). Think: Updateable means you may write.
wrong: `isAccessible()` checks read access, not edit access.
`isPermissionable()` only says whether field permissions can be set on the field.
`UserInfo` has no `canEdit()` method.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Schema.DescribeFieldResult / Enforcing Object and Field Permissions

questions.q: A developer needs Apex to give a specific user Edit access to a record of the custom object `Project__c`. Which object and fields are used?
options: `ProjectShare` with `RecordId`, `UserId`, `AccessLevel`
`Project__Share` with `ParentId`, `UserOrGroupId`, `AccessLevel`, `RowCause`
`Project__c` with `OwnerId` and a sharing reason picklist
`UserRecordAccess` with `RecordId` and `HasEditAccess`
questions.explain: A custom object's share rows live in `ObjectName__Share`. You set `ParentId` (the record), `UserOrGroupId` (who), `AccessLevel` (Read or Edit) and `RowCause` (why).
wrong: That is the wrong name and the wrong fields. Custom shares use `__Share`.
Changing the owner isn't sharing, and records have no sharing reason picklist.
`UserRecordAccess` is read-only. It reports access but can't grant it.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Understanding Sharing / Creating Apex Managed Sharing

questions.q: Apex creates share records so that the users listed on child `Team_Member__c` records can edit their `Project__c`. When a project's owner changes, the team members lose access. How should the developer fix this?
options: Insert the shares with `AccessLevel = 'All'`
Run the sharing code in a `without sharing` class so the shares can't be removed
Set the `Project__c` OWD to Public Read Only
Use a custom Apex sharing reason as the `RowCause`
questions.explain: Shares with `RowCause` **Manual** are deleted automatically when the owner changes. Shares with a custom **Apex sharing reason** stay. So give the code's shares an Apex sharing reason as their `RowCause`.
wrong: All is for the owner only, and access level doesn't protect against owner changes.
The class's sharing mode has nothing to do with surviving an owner change.
A wider OWD changes everyone's starting access and still doesn't keep Edit.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Apex Managed Sharing / Apex Sharing Reasons

questions.q: A developer tries to reference `Invoice__Share` in Apex, but the type doesn't exist. `Invoice__c` is a standalone custom object. What is the most likely cause?
options: `Invoice__c`'s organization-wide default is Public Read/Write
Apex managed sharing must first be enabled in a Permission Set
The class must be declared `without sharing` to reference share objects
Share objects are only available through the Metadata API
questions.explain: A custom object only gets a share object when its OWD is tighter than Public Read/Write. With **Public Read/Write**, everyone already has access, so `Invoice__Share` doesn't exist.
wrong: There is no permission set switch for Apex managed sharing.
Sharing keywords don't decide whether a type exists.
Share objects are normal sObjects you can query and save with DML.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Understanding Sharing

questions.q: This code runs in a trigger after a `Project__c` record is inserted. What is the result?
options: The share inserts and gives the user full access
The share inserts but `RowCause` defaults to Manual
The insert fails: Apex managed sharing can't grant `'All'`
The insert fails because `after insert` triggers can't create share records
questions.explain: Code can only grant **Read** or **Edit**. **All** (full access) is an internal level for the owner and users above them in the role hierarchy. No share row can grant it, so this insert fails.
wrong: A share row can't grant full access.
`RowCause` is set here on purpose, and the access level is invalid anyway.
Triggers can insert share rows. It's a common pattern.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Creating Apex Managed Sharing

questions.q: A team stores tax rates per country. The rates must move from sandbox to production with change sets, be used in a validation rule, and be read in Apex without using SOQL queries. What should the developer use?
options: A List custom setting
Custom labels
A custom object with a lookup
A custom metadata type
questions.explain: You need config that deploys, works in a validation rule and reads without SOQL. A **custom metadata type** does all three: its records are metadata, and `getAll()`/`getInstance()` use no SOQL.
wrong: Custom setting data doesn't travel in change sets.
Labels hold translatable text, not structured data per country.
Custom object data doesn't deploy, and reading it needs SOQL.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Custom Metadata Types

questions.q: A max-discount value must have an org-wide default. Sales Managers (a profile) get a higher value, and two specific users get personal overrides. Apex must read the right value for the running user without SOQL. What is the best solution?
options: A Hierarchy custom setting read with `Max_Discount__c.getInstance()`
A List custom setting keyed by profile name, read with `getValues()`
A custom metadata type with a Profile text field queried in SOQL
A custom label per profile
questions.explain: You need one value for the org, another for a profile and others for single users. A **Hierarchy custom setting** layers exactly that, and `getInstance()` returns the most specific value for the running user.
wrong: List settings don't pick values by user or profile on their own.
You'd need your own matching logic, and it has no built-in per-user override.
Labels hold translated text and can't vary by profile.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Custom Settings Methods (Hierarchy)

questions.q: A test method fails because `Integration_Config__c.getOrgDefaults()` returns no endpoint value. The same code works in the sandbox, where a value is set. `Integration_Config__c` is a hierarchy custom setting. What is the cause?
options: Custom settings can't be read in test context at all
`getOrgDefaults()` only works for List custom settings
The test needs `@IsTest(SeeAllData=false)` to see the org's custom setting records
Tests can't see org custom setting data, so the test must insert the setting
questions.explain: Tests can't see the org's data, and custom setting records count as data. So **the test must insert the setting** first, for example in test setup. Custom metadata, by contrast, is visible in tests.
wrong: Tests can read custom settings. They just need to create the data first.
`getOrgDefaults()` is a hierarchy custom setting method.
`SeeAllData=false` is the default, and it is what hides the data.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Isolation of Test Data from Organization Data in Unit Tests

questions.q: Which two statements about custom metadata types are true? (Choose 2)
options: Records can be created with standard `insert` DML in a trigger
Records can be read with `getAll()` and `getInstance()` without consuming SOQL queries
Apex can create or update records with `Metadata.Operations.enqueueDeployment()`, which runs asynchronously
Values resolve automatically by profile and then by user, like a hierarchy custom setting
Record data is excluded from change sets
questions.explain: Custom metadata reads are free and writes go through the Metadata API. `getAll()`/`getInstance()` use no SOQL, and Apex writes with `Metadata.Operations.enqueueDeployment()`, which runs later (async).
wrong: You can't use DML on `__mdt` records.
That describes hierarchy custom settings, not custom metadata.
Custom metadata records are metadata, so change sets can carry them.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Custom Metadata Types / Metadata Namespace

questions.q: An Apex error message shown to users must appear in each user's language. What should the developer use?
options: A custom label translated in Translation Workbench, read as `System.Label.Name`
A hard-coded string in each language selected with `if/else` on `UserInfo.getLanguage()`
A List custom setting with one record per language
A `static final String` constant
questions.explain: Text that must change with the user's language belongs in a **custom label**. Translate it in Translation Workbench, read `System.Label.Name`, and Salesforce picks the right language.
wrong: It works, but it's hard to maintain and skips the built-in translation tools.
A home-made translation table is possible, but it isn't the platform feature for this.
A constant can't be translated.
questions.source: Salesforce Help: Custom Labels

questions.q: A user's time zone is America/New_York (UTC-5 in January). What does this code most likely output?
questions.code:
Datetime dt = Datetime.newInstanceGmt(2026, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0);
System.debug(dt.format());
options: A string for 1 January 2026, 12:00 AM
A string for 31 December 2025, 7:00 PM, in the user's locale format
A string for 1 January 2026, 5:00 AM
An ISO string ending in Z
questions.explain: `format()` shows a GMT time in the user's own time zone and style. Midnight GMT on 1 January is **7:00 PM on 31 December** in New York (5 hours earlier).
wrong: That is the GMT time, which `formatGmt()` would show.
That shifts the time the wrong way.
`format()` gives a locale-style string, not an ISO 8601 string.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Datetime Class (format, newInstanceGmt)

questions.q: An ISV builds a managed package that must install in orgs with and without multi-currency. When multi-currency is enabled, the code must copy `CurrencyIsoCode` from the Opportunity to a custom object. What should the developer do?
options: Reference `opp.CurrencyIsoCode` directly and mark the package as requiring multi-currency
Use `convertCurrency()` in a static SOQL query in all orgs
Wrap the static reference in a `try/catch` for `TypeException`
Check `UserInfo.isMultiCurrencyOrganization()` and use dynamic SOQL with `get/put`
questions.explain: A direct `CurrencyIsoCode` reference won't even compile without multi-currency. So check `UserInfo.isMultiCurrencyOrganization()` at run time and reach the field dynamically with `get/put`.
wrong: Requiring multi-currency blocks single-currency orgs, which breaks the goal.
`convertCurrency()` needs multi-currency, and it doesn't copy the ISO code.
This is a compile-time problem, so `try/catch` can't help.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: UserInfo Class / Dynamic SOQL; Salesforce Help: Multiple Currencies

questions.q: A multilingual, multi-currency org needs a SOQL query that returns each opportunity's stage translated into the user's language and its amount formatted for the user's locale. Which two SOQL functions should be used? (Choose 2)
options: `toLabel(StageName)`
`convertTimezone(StageName)`
`FORMAT(Amount)`
`String.valueOf(Amount)`
`CALENDAR_MONTH(Amount)`
questions.explain: SOQL has one function for translated picklists and one for local formatting. `toLabel()` translates the stage, and `FORMAT()` formats the amount for the user's locale.
wrong: `convertTimezone()` only works on datetime fields inside date functions.
`String.valueOf` is Apex, not SOQL, and it ignores locale.
`CALENDAR_MONTH` is a date function, not a formatter.
questions.source: SOQL and SOSL Reference: toLabel(), FORMAT()

questions.q: Users in Tokyo say a monthly summary puts records created early on the 1st of the month into the previous month. The code uses the query below. What should the developer change?
questions.code:
SELECT CALENDAR_MONTH(CreatedDate) m, COUNT(Id) c
FROM Case
GROUP BY CALENDAR_MONTH(CreatedDate)
options: Call `Datetime.format()` on each `AggregateResult` to shift it to the user's time zone
Run the query in a `with sharing` class
Replace `CreatedDate` with `DAY_ONLY(CreatedDate)` in both `SELECT` and `GROUP BY`
Use `CALENDAR_MONTH(convertTimezone(CreatedDate))` in `SELECT` and `GROUP BY`
questions.explain: SOQL date functions read the clock in UTC unless you say otherwise. Wrapping the field as `CALENDAR_MONTH(convertTimezone(CreatedDate))` groups by the user's local time.
wrong: The grouping is already wrong before the results reach Apex.
Sharing has nothing to do with time zones.
`DAY_ONLY` also uses UTC unless it's wrapped in `convertTimezone()`.
questions.source: SOQL and SOSL Reference: Converting Time Zones in Date Functions

questions.q: A search page builds a SOQL string from text typed by the user. A security review flags SOQL injection. What is the most robust fix?
options: Run the query in a `with sharing` class
Strip all spaces from the input
Add `LIMIT 200` to the query
Use a bind variable, for example with `Database.queryWithBinds()`
questions.explain: Never let user text become part of the query itself. A **bind variable**, for example with `Database.queryWithBinds()`, passes the input as plain data. `String.escapeSingleQuotes()` is only a fallback.
wrong: Sharing doesn't stop someone changing the query's shape.
Injection doesn't need spaces, so this doesn't stop it.
A row limit doesn't stop an attacker rewriting the `WHERE` clause.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Dynamic SOQL / SOQL Injection

questions.q: A developer needs the ID of the Account record type with developer name "Partner" without using SOQL or hard-coding it. Which code works?
options: `Schema.SObjectType.Account.getRecordTypeInfosByDeveloperName().get('Partner').getRecordTypeId()`
`RecordType.getInstance('Partner').Id`
`Account.RecordTypeId.getDescribe().getDefaultValue()`
`UserInfo.getRecordTypeId('Account', 'Partner')`
questions.explain: Describe calls answer questions about your schema for free. `getRecordTypeInfosByDeveloperName().get('Partner').getRecordTypeId()` finds the ID with no SOQL.
wrong: `RecordType` has no `getInstance()` method.
This doesn't look up a record type by developer name.
`UserInfo` has no such method.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Schema.DescribeSObjectResult / RecordTypeInfo

questions.q: Discount rules change often. Admins want to pick which Apex class calculates discounts for each region by editing a custom metadata record that holds the class name. Each class implements `DiscountStrategy`. Which code correctly loads the right class?
options: `DiscountStrategy s = new cfg.Class_Name__c();`
`DiscountStrategy s = (DiscountStrategy) Type.forName(cfg.Class_Name__c).newInstance();`
`DiscountStrategy s = (DiscountStrategy) JSON.deserialize(cfg.Class_Name__c, DiscountStrategy.class);`
`DiscountStrategy s = Schema.getGlobalDescribe().get(cfg.Class_Name__c).newSObject();`
questions.explain: To create a class from a name stored as text, look it up at run time. `Type.forName()` finds the class, `newInstance()` creates it, and the cast gives you the interface. Check for `null` in case the name is wrong.
wrong: You can't use `new` with a text value.
Deserializing a class name doesn't create that class.
The global describe covers sObjects, not Apex classes.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Type Class / Strategy pattern

questions.q: What does this code print?
options: `true`, `true`
`false`, `false`
`true`, `false`
`false`, `true`
questions.explain: Apex Strings compare in two different ways. `==` ignores case, so it prints `true`. A `Set<String>` is case-sensitive, so `contains()` prints `false`.
wrong: `Set.contains()` is case-sensitive, so the second value is `false`.
`==` on Strings ignores case, so the first value is `true`.
The two results are the other way round.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Primitive Data Types (String) / Set Class

questions.q: A base class must provide a default shipping calculation that works on its own. Subclasses may optionally replace it. Code must be able to create the base class directly. How should it be declared?
options: `public abstract class Shipper { public abstract Decimal calc(); }`
`public interface Shipper { Decimal calc(); }`
`public class Shipper { public Decimal calc() {...} }`
`public virtual class Shipper { public virtual Decimal calc() {...} }`
questions.explain: You need a class you can create directly and children can change. A `virtual` class can be created and extended, and a `virtual` method gives a default body that children may `override`.
wrong: Abstract classes can't be created, and `abstract` methods have no default body.
Interfaces have no code and can't be created.
A plain class is `final`, so no child can extend it.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Extending a Class / Virtual and Abstract

questions.q: An org has three triggers on Opportunity written by different teams, and their order of execution is unpredictable. What best practice addresses this?
options: Add a `static Boolean` to each trigger
One trigger per object that delegates to a handler class
Move all the logic into a single `@future` method called from each trigger
Use the Trigger Order field to number the triggers
questions.explain: Several triggers on one object run in no guaranteed order. **One trigger per object** that hands off to a handler class lets you control the order, test easily and guard recursion in one place.
wrong: A static flag helps with recursion, not with order across triggers.
Async code changes behaviour (no before-save edits) and doesn't fix the design.
Apex triggers have no such field. Their order isn't guaranteed.
questions.source: Trailhead: Apex Triggers best practices; Apex Developer Guide: Triggers

questions.q: What happens when the developer saves `Child`?
options: It compiles; `Child` replaces `run()`
Compile error: `Parent` is not `virtual` or `abstract`, so it can't be extended
It compiles, but `Parent.run()` always executes at runtime
Compile error only because `Child` is missing the `override` keyword
questions.explain: Apex classes are `final` **by default**. `Parent` isn't `virtual` or `abstract`, so `Child` can't extend it, and the class doesn't compile.
wrong: Apex doesn't let you extend a `final` class.
The class never compiles, so nothing runs.
`override` is missing too, but the first error is that `Parent` can't be extended.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Extending a Class

questions.q: A team adopts the Apex Enterprise Patterns (service, domain, selector, unit of work). Which two responsibilities are assigned correctly? (Choose 2)
options: Selector layer: encapsulates SOQL queries for an object
Domain layer: owns all HTTP callouts for the org
Service layer: exposes business operations and defines the transaction boundary
Selector layer: performs all DML for the object
Unit of Work: executes each DML statement as soon as it is registered
questions.explain: Each enterprise layer has one job. The **Selector** holds an object's SOQL, and the **Service** offers business operations and owns the transaction.
wrong: Domain classes hold one object's logic and validation, not org-wide callouts.
DML is the unit of work's job, not the selector's.
The unit of work collects DML and commits it all later.
questions.source: Trailhead: Apex Enterprise Patterns (Service Layer, Domain & Selector Layers)

questions.q: Which declaration creates a valid custom exception?
options: `public class InventoryError extends Exception {}`
`public class InventoryException implements Exception {}`
`public class InventoryException extends Exception {}`
`public exception InventoryException {}`
questions.explain: A custom exception must **extend** `Exception` (a class, not an interface) and have a name ending in **Exception**. Only `InventoryException extends Exception` follows both rules.
wrong: The name must end in "Exception".
`Exception` is a class to extend, not an interface.
Apex has no `exception` keyword for declaring classes.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Create Custom Exceptions

questions.q: Review the code below. Which two statements are true after it runs? (Choose 2)
options: The `setSavepoint` and `rollback` calls don't count toward DML limits
The Contact remains in the database
`c.Id` still contains a value after the rollback
The Account remains in the database
The static counter is reset to 0
questions.explain: Rollback rewinds only the DML made after the savepoint. So the **Account stays**, and `c.Id` **keeps its value**, because IDs aren't cleared from rolled-back records.
wrong: Both `setSavepoint()` and `rollback()` count toward the DML statement limit.
The Contact was inserted after the savepoint, so it is undone.
Rollback never resets static variables.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Transaction Control

questions.q: A batch method sometimes hits "Too many SOQL queries: 101". A developer wraps the logic in `try/catch(Exception e)` to log the error and continue. What happens?
options: The `catch` block logs the error and processing continues
The `LimitException` can't be caught, and the transaction stops
Only the last query is rolled back
The platform retries the transaction automatically
questions.explain: Limit errors can't be caught. The `System.LimitException` skips every catch block and stops the transaction. Prevent it with bulkified code and checks like `Limits.getQueries()`.
wrong: Limit exceptions skip all catch blocks.
The whole transaction is rolled back, not just one query.
The platform never retries it for you.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Exception Statements / Execution Governors and Limits

questions.q: When importing 200 leads, one bad record must not stop the valid ones from saving. The developer also needs to know which records failed and why. What should be used?
options: `insert leads;` inside `try/catch`
`insert as user leads;`
`Database.setSavepoint()` before `insert leads;` then roll back only the failed rows
`Database.insert(leads, false)` and check each `SaveResult`
questions.explain: To keep the good rows and learn about the bad ones, allow partial success. `Database.insert(leads, false)` saves the valid records, and each `SaveResult` reports `isSuccess()` and `getErrors()`.
wrong: A plain insert is all-or-nothing, so one failure undoes the whole batch.
User mode checks permissions but is still all-or-nothing.
A savepoint undoes everything after it. It can't keep good rows or report errors.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Database Class Methods / SaveResult

questions.q: Which two statements about Platform Cache are true? (Choose 2)
options: Cached values can be evicted before their TTL expires, so code must handle a cache miss
Org cache values are guaranteed to persist for 48 hours
Org cache is visible only to the user who stored the value
Values stored in Platform Cache count against data storage
Session cache is tied to an individual user's session
questions.explain: The cache is a best-effort helper, not storage. Values **can be evicted early**, so code must handle a miss, and **session cache** belongs to one user's session.
wrong: 48 hours is the longest TTL, not a promise.
Org cache is shared by all users.
Cache uses partition space, not data storage.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Platform Cache

questions.q: Currency conversion rates are read thousands of times a day by all users and change once a day. A developer wants a single call that returns the cached rate, or loads it with SOQL and caches it on a miss. What should they build?
options: A `Cache.CacheBuilder` class with `doLoad()`, read via `Cache.Org.get(RateLoader.class, key)`
A Session cache entry populated by each user's first query
A `static Map` in a singleton class populated on first use
A hierarchy custom setting kept current by a trigger on `CurrencyType`, read with `getOrgDefaults()`
questions.explain: Data read by everyone and changed rarely belongs in org cache, loaded automatically on a miss. A `Cache.CacheBuilder` runs `doLoad()` on a miss and caches the result, all in one `Cache.Org.get()` call.
wrong: Session cache isn't shared, so every user would reload the rates.
Statics last only one transaction.
`CurrencyType` doesn't support Apex triggers, and a synced setting is more fragile than a self-loading cache.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: CacheBuilder Interface

questions.q: A singleton class caches a configuration map in a `private static` variable. Does the cached map carry over to the next, separate request from the same user?
options: Yes, a `private static` in a singleton persists for the rest of the user's session
Yes, for up to 24 hours
No, statics last one transaction. Use Platform Cache to share across requests
No, unless the class is declared `with sharing`
questions.explain: Static variables live for one transaction only. The next request starts fresh, so use **Platform Cache** (org or session) to keep data between requests.
wrong: That describes session cache, not statics.
24 hours is the org cache default TTL, not how statics behave.
Sharing keywords don't affect how long a static lives.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Static and Instance Methods, Variables / Platform Cache

questions.q: A developer is writing a utility class that is called from many places. It should run in the caller's sharing mode, and `with sharing` when it is the entry point of a transaction. Which declaration fits?
options: `public without sharing class RecordUtil`
`public inherited sharing class RecordUtil`
`public class RecordUtil` (no sharing keyword at all)
`public with sharing class RecordUtil`
questions.explain: You want the caller's mode, and `with sharing` when the class starts the request. That is `inherited sharing`, and it states the intent clearly.
wrong: This always ignores sharing, whoever calls it.
Classic rule: with no keyword, an entry point runs `without sharing`, so it isn't safe there.
This always enforces sharing, even when a `without sharing` class calls it.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Using the with sharing, without sharing, and inherited sharing Keywords

questions.q: A multi-currency org stores opportunities in several currencies. Which field tells Apex which currency an Opportunity's `Amount` is in?
options: `DefaultCurrencyIsoCode` on the Opportunity record
`CurrencyType`, a lookup on each record to the currency
`CurrencyIsoCode` on the Opportunity record
`UserInfo.getDefaultCurrency()` for the record owner
questions.explain: In a multi-currency org every record names its own currency. The `CurrencyIsoCode` field on the Opportunity says which currency `Amount` is in.
wrong: `DefaultCurrencyIsoCode` is the user's personal currency, on the User record.
`CurrencyType` lists the org's currencies and rates. Records don't look it up.
That is the running user's currency, which may differ from the record's.
questions.source: Salesforce Help: Manage Multiple Currencies; Object Reference: CurrencyType

questions.q: A logging utility receives record Ids from many objects (Accounts, Cases, custom objects) and must branch on the object type. It is called in loops, so it must be cheap. What should the developer use?
options: `recordId.getSObjectType()`, then compare it with tokens like `Account.SObjectType`
Query each candidate object with `WHERE Id = :recordId` until one of the queries returns a row
Loop over `Schema.getGlobalDescribe()` and compare each object's `getKeyPrefix()` with the Id's prefix
Compare `String.valueOf(recordId).left(3)` with key prefixes hard-coded for each object
questions.explain: Every Id already knows its object. `recordId.getSObjectType()` returns the token, like `Account.SObjectType`, with no query and no global describe, so it's cheap in loops.
wrong: This wastes SOQL queries and fails for objects you didn't list.
It works, but a global describe is expensive, especially inside a loop.
Custom object key prefixes differ between orgs, so hard-coded ones break.
questions.source: Apex Reference Guide: Id Class (getSObjectType)

questions.q: A developer adds a payment provider that implements an existing interface. What happens when `CardPay` is saved?
options: It compiles, because interface methods take the class's default access
It compiles, and `charge()` stays `private` to `CardPay` as declared
Compile error: `CardPay` must also be declared `virtual` to implement an interface
Compile error: the implementation of `charge()` must be `public` or `global`
questions.explain: A method that fulfils an interface must be `public` or `global`. With no modifier an Apex method is `private`, so `CardPay` doesn't compile.
wrong: Default access is `private`, which doesn't match the interface, so it's rejected.
An interface method can't be `private`, so the class doesn't compile.
Implementing an interface doesn't need `virtual`. Virtual is about being extended.
questions.source: Apex Developer Guide: Interfaces; Access Modifiers

questions.q: A service catches a `DmlException` and must throw its own `OrderException`, keeping the original error as the cause for logging. Which line does this?
options: `throw (OrderException) e;`
`throw new OrderException(e.getMessage() + e.getCause());`
`throw new OrderException('Order save failed', e);`
`throw new OrderException('Order save failed').setCause(e);`
questions.explain: Every custom exception gets a free (message, cause) constructor. `new OrderException('Order save failed', e)` keeps the original error, which callers read with `getCause()`.
